intro.promise: By the end you’ll be able to rank concepts with a weighted matrix, and test whether the winner survives changes in the weights.
intro.whyItMatters: A decision that records its weights and scores can be discussed, challenged and defended.

recap.keyIdea: A weighted matrix multiplies scores by weights fixed in advance and adds them, and a sensitivity check shows whether the winner is robust or only close.

blocks.text: You turned a brief into four weighted criteria, scored two concepts and found totals of 3.7 for A and 3.9 for B. Swapping two weights left B ahead at 4.1 to 3.6, but weighting cost at 0.6 made A the winner, and the two totals are equal when cost carries a weight of 0.5.
The total is a way of exposing the assumptions behind a choice, and the sensitivity check shows which of them the choice depends on. With this, a team can state what it chose and why.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a need, not a solution?
hints: Ask whether a quite different product could still satisfy the sentence.
A need describes what happens to the soup, not what the container is made of.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence fits a flask, a heated pot or a thick-walled bowl, which is what marks it as a need. The three others each fix one construction.

misconceptions.feedback: A vacuum flask is one way to keep soup hot, so it is a solution. The need is the temperature the soup must hold, which another container could also meet.
A steel lid is one part of one design. Many designs have lids and still let the soup go cold, so it does not say what the person needs.
A screw top is a way of closing a container, so it is a solution. Other closures might serve the person just as well.

choices.label: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour

acceptedIdeas: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep soup above 60 C for an hour

questions.prompt: Another request says the kettle has a clear window in its side. Which need is that sentence standing in for?
hints: Ask what the person could not do if the kettle had no window at all.
The need describes what the person is trying to find out before switching on.
questions.onCorrect: Once the need is stated, a gauge on the handle or marks inside the jug becomes an option that the window sentence had ruled out.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing in the sentence concerns the material of the body. The window is there so that the person can learn something before boiling.
The window is in the side, so the size of the lid has nothing to do with it. Ask what the person looks through the window to find out.
Appearance is not what a window in the side is for. Ask what the person could not tell without it.

choices.label: The kettle should look the same as the old one
The user can see how much water is inside before switching on
The lid should be as small as possible
The kettle should be made of plastic

acceptedIdeas: The user can see how much water is inside before switching on
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The user can see how much water is inside before switching on

questions.prompt: A delivery takes 90 minutes, and the team wants a margin of 30 minutes before the customer opens the bag. For how many hours must the food stay below 5 C?
hints: Add the margin to the delivery time first.
Both times are in minutes, so convert the total to hours.
Divide the total number of minutes by 60.
questions.onCorrect: The requirement now reads: keep the food at or below 5 C for 2 hours. It does not mention foam, ice packs or any other construction.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the delivery time alone. The margin of 30 minutes has to be added before converting to hours.
That is the number of minutes. The question asks for hours.

questions.prompt: A kettle is required to heat 1 litre of water (1 kg) from 20 C to 100 C in 2 minutes. Taking 4.19 kJ per kilogram per degree, what is the least heating power in watts, ignoring all losses?
hints: Find the energy first: mass times 4.19 times the temperature rise.
The temperature rise is 100 − 20 = 80 degrees, and 2 minutes is 120 seconds.
Power in kilowatts is energy in kilojoules divided by time in seconds. Convert to watts.
questions.onCorrect: A shorter time raises the power needed in proportion, so a numbered requirement tells the designer how big the heating element must be.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power for 3 minutes. This requirement allows 2 minutes, which is 120 seconds.
That is the energy in kilojoules. Divide by the time in seconds to get power.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Energy = 4.19 × 80 = 335.2 kJ. Over 120 s, power = 335.2 / 120 = 2.793 kW, which is about 2793 W.

questions.prompt: The Double Diamond has two diamonds: discover then define, and develop then ___.
hints: The four phases all begin with the letter D.
The last phase ends with a tested design ready to be made.
questions.onCorrect: Deliver is the last phase, where one tested design is chosen and prepared for making.

questions.prompt: How many times does the Double Diamond widen, counting each time the shape opens out from a point?
hints: Look at the shape, not at the phase names.
Each diamond opens out and then closes in.
Count the diamonds.
questions.onCorrect: The process widens to gather possibilities and narrows to decide, first for the problem and then for the solution.

misconceptions.feedback: One diamond widens once, and there are two diamonds.
There are four phases, but each diamond widens once and narrows once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shape widens once in discover and once in develop, so twice.

questions.prompt: The Double Diamond widens twice. Which two phases are the widenings?
hints: Each diamond opens out and then closes in.
Look for the phase that opens each diamond, the one that gathers possibilities.
questions.onCorrect: The team widens once to learn about the problem and once to generate answers to it, and narrows after each.

misconceptions.feedback: Define and deliver are the two narrowings, in which the team chooses one problem and then settles on one design.
Discover widens the view of the problem and define narrows it again, so together they make the whole first diamond.
Develop widens the range of possible answers and deliver narrows them to one tested design, so together they make the whole second diamond.

questions.prompt: Eight people each take a 250 ml cup of hot water in one round. How many litres must the kettle hold?
hints: Multiply the cup size by the number of people.
Work in millilitres, then convert.
1000 ml make one litre.
questions.onCorrect: Capacity is the first number a problem statement for the kettle can carry, and it comes from the people, not from a kettle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the volume in millilitres. The question asks for litres.
That is one cup. Multiply by the eight people.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a phone case with a raised rim. Which sentence states a need?
hints: Ask whether a design without a rim could satisfy the sentence.
Look for the sentence that says what happens to the phone, with a number.
questions.onCorrect: The sentence names a fall, a surface and a height, so a prototype can be dropped and judged against it, whatever it is built from.

misconceptions.feedback: A 2 mm rim is a way of protecting the screen, so it is a solution. The need is what the rim has to achieve.
A material is a choice about how to build the case. The need says what the case must do for the person.
Rounded corners are one feature of one design. The sentence says nothing about what the person needs.

choices.label: Round the corners of the case
Protect the screen when the phone lands face down on a hard floor from 1 m
Add a 2 mm rim all round the screen

acceptedIdeas: Protect the screen when the phone lands face down on a hard floor from 1 m
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Protect the screen when the phone lands face down on a hard floor from 1 m

questions.prompt: A statement of what must happen for the person, leaving out how a design achieves it, is called a ___.
hints: The opposite of a solution.
questions.onCorrect: A need leaves several designs open, which is why it comes before the concepts.

misconceptions.feedback: A solution says how. The word wanted names what must happen, however it is done.

questions.prompt: A kettle must heat 1.5 litres (1.5 kg) from 20 C to 100 C in under 4 minutes. Taking 4.19 kJ per kilogram per degree, what is the least heating power in watts, ignoring losses?
hints: Energy is mass times 4.19 times the temperature rise of 80 degrees.
4 minutes is 240 seconds.
Divide the energy in kilojoules by the time in seconds, then convert kilowatts to watts.
questions.onCorrect: More water in the same kind of time asks for a larger element, or for more time, so capacity and speed have to be chosen together.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 1 litre and 3 minutes. Use the 1.5 litres and the 240 seconds given here.
That is the energy in kilojoules. Divide by the time in seconds.

questions.prompt: In the Double Diamond, which phase turns what the team found into a clear statement of the problem?
hints: It is the second phase, where the first diamond narrows.
questions.onCorrect: Define ends the first diamond with a brief, so the second diamond can begin with a problem that has been chosen.

misconceptions.feedback: Discover collects observations and does not yet choose among them. The phase wanted narrows them to one problem.

questions.prompt: A kettle lid has a small raised arrow that shows where to press to open it. The arrow is the lid’s ___.
hints: The lid can be opened whether or not the arrow is there. What does the arrow add?
The word begins with "sign".
questions.onCorrect: A signifier is the part of the design that can be seen, heard or felt, so a designer can change it without changing what the object can do.

misconceptions.feedback: The affordance is that the lid can be opened at all. The arrow is the cue that shows where to press.

questions.prompt: Four knobs control four burners, and any knob could be wired to any burner, one knob to one burner. Roughly how many different wirings are possible?
hints: Count the burners the first knob could go to, then the burners left for the second.
The choices multiply.
questions.onCorrect: The exact figure is 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24, since each knob has one fewer burner left to choose from than the knob before it.

misconceptions.feedback: Four is the number of knobs. The first knob can go to any of four burners, the second to any of the three left, and so on, which gives many more wirings than there are knobs.
The choices multiply rather than add: four burners for the first knob, three for the second, two for the third and one for the last give 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
The count grows quickly, but four knobs give 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24, and it takes five knobs to pass 100.

questions.prompt: Now a cooker has five rings and five knobs, again one knob to one ring. How many assignments are there?
hints: The number of choices falls by one with each knob placed.
Start at 5 and count down to 1.
Multiply 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
questions.onCorrect: Each extra knob multiplies the count, so a layout that has to be memorised gets harder to learn very quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 5 × 5, which lets two knobs share a ring. Each ring takes one knob, so the choices fall by one each time.
That is the count for four knobs. A fifth knob multiplies it by 5.

questions.prompt: You press a lift’s call button and the ring around it lights up. That light is the button’s ___.
hints: The light comes after the press, not before it.
questions.onCorrect: Feedback closes the loop: without it a user cannot tell whether a press registered or whether to press again.

misconceptions.feedback: A signifier shows what can be done before the action. The light comes after the press and tells you it registered.
Mapping links a control to what it affects. The light is the response you perceive after pressing.

questions.prompt: You mean to turn on the hall light, but your hand flips the switch beside it, which turns on the porch light. Is this a slip or a mistake?
hints: Was your goal right?
The goal was right and the hand went to the wrong switch.
questions.onCorrect: A slip is a right goal carried out wrongly, so it is reduced by making the wrong action harder, for example by spacing the switches or mapping them to the lights they control.

misconceptions.feedback: In a mistake the goal itself is wrong. Here the goal, the hall light, was right and the hand landed on the wrong switch.

questions.prompt: With no cue at all and four knobs in a row, a user guesses which knob lights the front-left burner. The chance of being right is 1 in how many?
hints: One burner, one correct knob.
Count the knobs the user chooses among.
Chance = number of correct knobs divided by number of knobs.
questions.onCorrect: A wrong guess is then a slip, with the right goal and the wrong knob, which the layout invited.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of ways of wiring four knobs, not the number of knobs the user chooses among.
That would be certain. The user is choosing among four knobs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One of the four knobs is right, so the chance is 1 in 4.

questions.prompt: Three ceiling lights in a line are controlled by three switches in a row on the wall, wired in a different order from the lights. Which change gives the natural mapping?
hints: Natural mapping uses position, so look for the answer that does.
Ask what the user could do without reading anything.
questions.onCorrect: When the switches follow the order of the lights, the layout itself says which is which, and the labels become unnecessary.

misconceptions.feedback: A label has to be read and compared with the lights on every use. The order of the switches could say it without reading.
Colours would have to be learnt for each switch. They do not relate the switches to where the lights are.
A sign adds something to learn and read. A natural mapping needs nothing to read, because position carries the information.

choices.label: Make the switches three different colours
Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights
Add a printed label beside each switch
Fit a sign explaining the wiring

acceptedIdeas: Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wire the switches in the same left-to-right order as the lights

questions.prompt: A hob has six burners and six knobs, one knob to one burner. How many assignments are there?
hints: The choices fall by one with each knob placed.
Start at 6 and count down to 1.
Multiply 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1.
questions.onCorrect: Six burners already give 720 wirings, so no one can rely on memory for an arbitrary layout.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 6 × 6, which lets two knobs share a burner.
That is the count for five burners. Multiply it by 6.

questions.prompt: A cook follows a recipe that misprints 250 C for 150 C and sets the oven to 250 C, as written. The goal itself was wrong because of the unclear recipe. Is this a slip or a mistake?
hints: Was the goal itself wrong, or only the action?
questions.onCorrect: A mistake comes from a wrong goal or plan, so the fix lies in clearer information, not in spacing controls apart.

misconceptions.feedback: In a slip the goal is right and the action goes wrong. Here the cook did what the recipe said, and the recipe was wrong.

questions.prompt: What an object makes possible for a person, whether or not it can be seen, is its ___.
hints: It is the possible action, not the visible cue.
questions.onCorrect: A chair affords sitting even in the dark, and a signifier is what lets a person see that it does.

misconceptions.feedback: A signifier is the cue that shows it. The word wanted names the possibility itself.

questions.prompt: A shelf is meant to be reached by most users. A percentile of reach is the reach that a given share of people are at or below, so the 5th percentile is the reach that 5 percent of people are at or below. Which percentile of reach should the shelf height be set from?
hints: Who is the first person to be left out of reach: someone with a long reach or a short one?
The design has to suit the people with the shortest reach.
questions.onCorrect: A shelf at the 5th percentile of reach can be reached by 95 percent of users, since everyone with a longer reach reaches it as well.

misconceptions.feedback: Set from the median, the shelf would be out of reach for about half of the users, since half have a shorter reach.
A shelf set from a long reach is out of reach for everyone whose reach is shorter, which is nearly all the users.
The 99th percentile is longer still, so nearly everyone would fall short of the shelf.

questions.prompt: A body measure has a mean of 920 mm and a standard deviation of 35 mm (illustrative values). What is its 95th percentile, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: The 95th percentile is the mean plus 1.645 standard deviations.
Work out 1.645 × 35 first.
Add the result to 920.
questions.onCorrect: About 95 percent of people have this measure at or below 978 mm, so the 5 percent above it are the part the design would leave out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean plus one standard deviation, which is about the 84th percentile. The 95th is 1.645 standard deviations above the mean.
That multiplies the whole figure out of place. Add 1.645 × 35 to 920.

questions.prompt: The 95th percentile of stature is 1865 mm. A doorway is to clear that height with a margin of 100 mm. What is the doorway height, in millimetres?
hints: A doorway is a clearance, so it must suit the tall end of the range.
Add the margin to the 95th percentile.
questions.onCorrect: A doorway at 1965 mm lets 95 percent of adults walk through with the margin to spare, and the rest can be helped by a taller opening where it matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the mean stature. A clearance has to suit the tall end, not the middle.
That puts the margin on the mean instead of the 95th percentile.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The clearance is set from the large end: 1865 + 100 = 1965 mm.

questions.prompt: A control must be reachable by 95 percent of users. Their overhead reach has a mean of 640 mm and a standard deviation of 30 mm above the shoulder (illustrative). What is the 5th percentile of this reach, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: For the 5th percentile, subtract from the mean.
Work out 1.645 × 30.
Subtract that from 640.
questions.onCorrect: Placing the control within 591 mm lets the shortest 5 percent just reach it, and everyone with a longer reach reaches it too.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 95th percentile. A reach has to be set from the short end, the 5th.
That is the mean minus one standard deviation, the 16th percentile. Use 1.645 standard deviations for the 5th.

questions.prompt: A seat height is to adjust to suit people from the 5th to the 95th percentile of popliteal height, the height of the back of the knee above the floor when seated. Its mean is 430 mm and its standard deviation 25 mm (illustrative). How far apart, in millimetres, are those two heights, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: Take the 95th percentile minus the 5th.
The difference is 2 × 1.645 × 25.
questions.onCorrect: An adjustable feature has to cover that span, and anything fixed at one height can serve only the people near it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is half the span, from the mean to one end. The span runs from the 5th to the 95th.
That is one standard deviation. The span is 3.29 standard deviations wide.

questions.prompt: The recommended weight limit for a lift is 23 kg × 0.7 × 0.9, and the load is 12 kg. What is the lifting index, to two decimals?
hints: First multiply 23 by both multipliers to find the limit.
The limit is 14.49 kg.
Divide the 12 kg load by the limit.
questions.onCorrect: An index under 1.0 means the load is within the recommended limit for that lift.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses a different lift, with a 20 kg load and a limit of 16.56 kg. Work out the limit for these multipliers.
That is the recommended limit. The lifting index divides the load by it.

questions.prompt: The same lift is repeated from a lower start, and the multipliers fall to 0.7 and 0.9. What is the greatest load, in kilograms, that keeps the lifting index at 1.0?
hints: An index of 1.0 means the load equals the recommended limit.
Multiply 23 by 0.7 and by 0.9.
questions.onCorrect: Each multiplier below 1 lowers the limit, so a worse posture lowers the load that is acceptable.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit for the earlier multipliers of 0.8 and 0.9. These multipliers are smaller.
That is the starting limit before any multiplier is applied.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The index is 1.0 when the load equals the limit: 23 × 0.7 × 0.9 = 14.49 kg.

questions.prompt: Stature has a mean of 1750 mm and a standard deviation of 70 mm (illustrative). What is the 5th percentile, to the nearest millimetre?
hints: The 5th percentile lies below the mean.
Work out 1.645 × 70.
Subtract it from 1750.
questions.onCorrect: About 5 percent of people are shorter than this, which makes it the starting point for a design that must suit short users.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 95th percentile. The 5th lies below the mean.
That is the mean minus one standard deviation. Use 1.645 standard deviations.

questions.prompt: The size that 95 percent of people are at or below is called the 95th ___.
hints: The word is used for any share, such as the 5th or the 50th.
questions.onCorrect: A percentile names a place in the spread of people and is not a particular person.

questions.prompt: A lift has a recommended limit of 23 × 0.75 × 0.8 kg, and the load is 18 kg. What is the lifting index, to two decimals?
hints: Find the limit first: 23 multiplied by both multipliers.
The limit is 13.8 kg.
Divide 18 by 13.8.
questions.onCorrect: An index above 1.0 means the lift exceeds the recommended limit, so it should be redesigned or the load reduced.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the limit by the load. The index is load divided by limit.
That is the limit. Divide the 18 kg load by it.

questions.prompt: A button 160 mm from the cursor is either 20 mm wide or 10 mm wide. Which is slower to hit?
hints: Think about how carefully the hand must finish its movement.
A narrow target leaves less room for error.
questions.onCorrect: Both the distance and the width matter, and the next screen puts them into one number.

misconceptions.feedback: The wider button is the easier target, because a larger target tolerates a less exact movement. It is the narrower one that needs the careful final approach.
The distance is the same, but the width is not. A narrower target asks for a more careful movement, and that takes time.

questions.prompt: A button is 300 mm from the cursor and 20 mm wide. What is its index of difficulty ID = log2(D/W + 1), in bits?
hints: Divide the distance by the width first.
Add 1 to the ratio, which gives 16.
16 is 2 raised to what power?
questions.onCorrect: The ID is in bits because it is a base-2 logarithm, and 16 is 2 to the power 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is close to log2(15). The formula adds 1 to D/W before taking the logarithm.
That is D/W, the ratio before the logarithm. Add 1 and take log2.

questions.prompt: A button is 240 mm away and 40 mm wide. Taking a = 0.1 s and b = 0.15 s per bit (illustrative), what is the predicted movement time, in seconds, to two decimals?
hints: Find the ID first: D/W = 6, plus 1.
ID = log2(7), which is about 2.81.
questions.onCorrect: A time of about half a second is typical for a short reach to a large button, and the constants vary with the device.

misconceptions.feedback: That is b × ID alone, without the constant a. MT = a + b × ID.
That is the ID in bits. Multiply by b and add a to get seconds.

questions.prompt: A button 300 mm away is 30 mm wide, then narrowed to 15 mm. By how many bits does the ID rise, to two decimals?
hints: Work out the ID for each width.
Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: Each halving of the width costs about one bit, about 0.14 s with these constants, so many small targets cost much more than a few large ones.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the limit for a long way off, where halving the width adds exactly one bit. The +1 inside the logarithm makes the rise a little less here.
Halving the width does not halve the ID. It adds about one bit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ID rises from log2(300/30 + 1) = log2(11) = 3.46 to log2(300/15 + 1) = log2(21) = 4.39, a rise of 0.93 bits, which is nearly one.

questions.prompt: A menu grows from 7 items to 15 items. By Hick’s law, how does the choice time change?
hints: Ask whether the time grows in proportion to the items.
Time depends on log2(n + 1).
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the options adds about one bit of choice, which is a fixed time b, and not a doubling of the whole time.

misconceptions.feedback: Choice time depends on the logarithm of the number of options, not on the number itself, so doubling the items does not double the time.
More options do cost time, but the cost is small and steady: each doubling adds one step.

choices.label: It rises by one fixed step

acceptedIdeas: It rises by one fixed step
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It rises by one fixed step

questions.prompt: Using the same Hick constant, b = 0.2 s, what is the choice time for 31 equally likely options?
hints: Add 1 to the number of options first.
32 is 2 to the power 5.
Multiply 5 by 0.2 s.
questions.onCorrect: Going from 15 to 31 options added just one step of 0.2 s, which is why long menus cost less time than they seem to.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies b by the number of options. Choice time depends on log2(n + 1).
That is the time for 15 options. 31 options give log2(32) = 5 bits.

questions.prompt: A target sits at the edge of the screen, where the cursor stops, so its effective width is 200 mm instead of 20 mm. For D = 160 mm, a = 0.1 s and b = 0.15 s per bit, what is the movement time in seconds, to two decimals?
hints: The ratio D/W is now 160 divided by 200.
ID = log2(1.8), which is about 0.85.
questions.onCorrect: The screen edge acts as a target of very great depth, which is why menus and buttons placed there are so quick to hit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for a 20 mm target. At the screen edge the effective width is 200 mm.
That is the ID in bits. Multiply by b and add a for the time.

questions.prompt: A target is 160 mm away and 20 mm wide. What is its index of difficulty, in bits, to two decimals?
hints: Divide D by W and add 1.
The ratio plus 1 is 9.
Take log2 of 9.
questions.onCorrect: A smaller ratio of distance to width gives a smaller ID, and so a quicker movement.

misconceptions.feedback: That is log2(8). The formula uses D/W + 1, which is 9.
That is D/W. Add 1 and take log2.

questions.prompt: With b = 0.3 s, what is the Hick choice time for 15 equally likely options, in seconds?
hints: Add 1 to the number of options.
16 is 2 to the power 4.
Multiply 4 by 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: The time grows with the logarithm, so more options always cost something but cost less and less per option.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies b by the number of options. Use log2(n + 1).
That uses log2(8), which belongs to 7 options. Add 1 to 15 first.

questions.prompt: The law that predicts the time to point at a target from its distance and width is named after ___.
hints: It was published in 1954, and the name is that of its author.
questions.onCorrect: Fitts’s law models movement time as a straight-line function of the index of difficulty.

misconceptions.feedback: Hick’s law concerns the time to choose among options. The law for pointing at a target is named after another person.

questions.prompt: A smoke alarm sounds a loud tone and also flashes a bright light when it detects smoke. Which of the seven principles of universal design is this?
hints: Ask what the tone and the light have in common.
One principle is about communicating by more than one sense.
questions.onCorrect: A person who cannot hear the tone sees the light, and one asleep facing the wall hears the tone, so the warning reaches both.

misconceptions.feedback: Low physical effort concerns how little force and fatigue a design asks for. The tone and the light ask no effort either way, and what they add is a second sense.
Tolerance for error limits the harm of accidents and mistakes. The tone and the light carry the same warning by sound and by sight.
Size and space concerns room to reach, approach and operate a design, while the tone and the light concern how information reaches the person.

choices.label: Size and space for approach and use

questions.prompt: The 2010 ADA Standards give the running slope of a ramp as at most 1:12. What does this mean for a designer?
hints: Read the ratio as rise to run.
A limit is the most that is allowed.
questions.onCorrect: The ratio is a limit on steepness, and many people find even this slope hard work, so a gentler one is better where space allows.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a slope twelve times steeper than the horizontal, which is a wall rather than a ramp. In 1:12, the 12 is the distance along.
The ratio does not fix the length, since a ramp for a small rise can be much shorter. It fixes how much length each unit of rise needs.
The figure of 1:12 is a limit, not a target. A gentler slope is better for the people who climb it.

choices.label: A ramp must be at least 12 m long
A ramp may rise 1 unit for every 12 along, and no steeper
A ramp must rise 12 units for every 1 along
A ramp should be as steep as 1:12 to save space

acceptedIdeas: A ramp may rise 1 unit for every 12 along, and no steeper
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A ramp may rise 1 unit for every 12 along, and no steeper

questions.prompt: The unobstructed forward reach range is 380 mm to 1220 mm above the floor. A switch is fitted at 1500 mm. By how many millimetres is it above the top of the range?
hints: Which end of the range is the switch beyond?
The upper limit is 1220 mm.
Subtract it from 1500 mm.
questions.onCorrect: A switch beyond the upper limit cannot be reached from a seated position by many users, so it is placed lower, within the range.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the height of the switch above the bottom of the range. The question asks how far it is above the top.
That mixes up the numbers. Take the top of the range, 1220 mm, from the height of the switch.

questions.prompt: A kerb rises 0.45 m to a door. At a slope of 1:12, what horizontal run is needed, in metres?
hints: Each 1 m of rise needs 12 m of run.
Multiply the rise by 12.
questions.onCorrect: A small rise still needs a long run, so a ramp often decides where the entrance is placed.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 12. Each unit of rise needs 12 units of run, so multiply.
That is the run for a rise of 1 m. Multiply 12 by 0.45.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each metre of rise needs 12 m of run: 0.45 × 12 = 5.4 m.

questions.prompt: A porch is 0.9 m above the path. What is the shortest horizontal run, in metres, for a ramp at a slope of 1:12?
hints: A slope of 1:12 needs 12 units of run for every unit of rise.
Multiply the rise by 12.
questions.onCorrect: Rises above about 0.75 m are often handled with a ramp that turns back on itself, because the straight run becomes very long.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 0.9 by 12. Multiply the rise by 12.
That is the run for a rise of 0.6 m, not 0.9 m.

questions.prompt: The least clear width of a door opening is 815 mm. How many inches is that, to the nearest whole inch?
hints: There are 25.4 mm in an inch.
An inch is longer than a millimetre, so the answer is smaller than 815.
Divide 815 by 25.4.
questions.onCorrect: The two units describe the same width, and a drawing should say which one it uses.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the width in millimetres. Divide by 25.4 to get inches.
That multiplies instead of dividing. An inch is longer than a millimetre, so there are fewer inches.

questions.prompt: A door leaf is 850 mm wide, but when it is open the gap between the door and the opposite stop is 790 mm. Does the opening meet the 815 mm clear width in the 2010 ADA Standards?
hints: Clear width is the gap left when the door is open.
Compare the gap, not the leaf, with 815 mm.
questions.onCorrect: The leaf width is the number a catalogue lists, while the clear width is what a wheelchair meets, so a drawing has to be checked against the second.

misconceptions.feedback: The leaf width is the size of the door itself. Clear width is measured between the open door and the opposite stop, and here that gap is only 790 mm.
The 815 mm figure is a minimum, so an opening 25 mm narrower falls short of it, however small the difference looks.
The requirement concerns width alone, and the 790 mm gap is already below the 815 mm minimum.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the clear width is 790 mm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the clear width is 790 mm

choices.label: Yes, because 790 mm is within 5 percent of 815 mm
No, because the clear width is 790 mm
It cannot be said without the height of the door
Yes, because the leaf is wider than 815 mm

questions.prompt: A ramp can have a horizontal run of only 6 m. At a slope of 1:12 at most, what is the greatest rise it can cover, in metres?
hints: The rise is a twelfth of the run at the steepest allowed slope.
Divide the run by 12.
questions.onCorrect: Working backwards from the space available is how a designer finds out whether a ramp will fit, before drawing it.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 12. Here the run is known and the rise is wanted, so divide.
That is the run itself. Divide by 12 to find the rise.

questions.prompt: Large handles that need little force serve which of the seven principles of universal design?
hints: Think about what a large handle saves the person.
One principle is about force and fatigue.
questions.onCorrect: A handle that needs little force also serves anyone with full hands, cold fingers or a weak grip, which is the pattern of universal design.

misconceptions.feedback: Perceptible information concerns communicating by more than one sense. A large handle is about the force needed to use it.
Tolerance for error limits the harm of accidents and mistakes, while a large, easy handle reduces the force and fatigue of every use.
Simple and intuitive use concerns how easily a design is understood. A handle that needs little force is about the body, not about understanding.

questions.prompt: A socket is fitted at 250 mm above the floor. By how many millimetres is it below the bottom of the forward reach range of 380 to 1220 mm?
hints: Find the lower limit of the range.
The socket is lower than that limit.
Take the socket height from the lower limit.
questions.onCorrect: A socket this low can be reached only by bending, so it is raised within the range.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the distance from the socket to the top of the range. The question asks about the bottom.
That is the top of the range. The socket is below the bottom limit.

questions.prompt: A step rises 0.3 m. What is the shortest horizontal run for a ramp at a slope of 1:12, in metres?
hints: A slope of 1:12 needs 12 units of run for each unit of rise.
Multiply the rise by 12.
questions.onCorrect: A small step still needs several metres of ramp, so the ramp is planned together with the entrance.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 12. Multiply the rise by 12.
That is the run for a rise of 0.6 m.

questions.prompt: Which of these came first?
hints: Think of the earliest process: steam-bending wood in a factory.
Industrial design began with industry, long before electronics.
questions.onCorrect: Industrial production of furniture in 1859 is an early example of design shaped by a process, a theme that returns in every later landmark.

misconceptions.feedback: The Braun SK 4 was designed in 1956, nearly a century after the chair that came first in this list.
The Bauhaus was founded in 1919, which is later than the bentwood chair on this list.
The first iPhone appeared in 2007. Industrial design was long established by then, and did not begin with computers.

questions.prompt: Thonet shipped 36 chairs in each cubic metre. How many cubic metres does a shipment of 360 chairs need?
hints: Each cubic metre holds 36 chairs.
Divide the number of chairs by 36.
questions.onCorrect: Flat-packing is a way of making the form serve the shipping, and it was part of the design from the start.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the space for 36 chairs. A shipment of 360 chairs is ten times as many.
That multiplies instead of dividing. Each cubic metre holds 36 chairs, so divide the total by 36.

questions.prompt: A bookcase sold today as flat boards in a box, to be put together at home, follows the same idea as Thonet’s No. 14. Which part of the chair’s story does it share?
hints: Think about how the No. 14 reached its buyers.
Parts pack more tightly than a finished piece of furniture.
questions.onCorrect: In both, the product is designed as parts that pack flat, and the form follows from how it is shipped as well as how it is made.

misconceptions.feedback: The No. 14 was an ordinary size, and the bookcase is not small either. What they share is travelling in pieces, which pack far more tightly than finished furniture.
The No. 14 was packed before it was assembled, as a few bent parts, and the bookcase is packed as boards in the same way.
The No. 14 was made of beech, and the weight of a wood has no bearing on how many pieces fit in a given volume.

acceptedIdeas: The chair travelled as a few parts and was assembled where it was sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The chair travelled as a few parts and was assembled where it was sold

choices.label: The chair was made of a lighter wood than beech
The finished chairs stacked inside one another
The chair travelled as a few parts and was assembled where it was sold
The chair was smaller than most chairs of the time

questions.prompt: The Thonet No. 14 chair dates from 1859 and the Braun SK 4 from 1956. How many years apart are they?
hints: Subtract the earlier year from the later.
From 1859 to 1900 is 41 years.
Add the 56 years from 1900 to 1956.
questions.onCorrect: Industrial design therefore has a history of well over a century, which is longer than the history of electronics.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 1859 to 1956 in the wrong places. Subtract the earlier year from the later.
That is a slip in the subtraction. Work from 1859 to 1956 in two steps through 1900.

questions.prompt: A chair seat curves in two directions at once and is made from a single piece of wood. Which of these landmarks used the process that can give such a shape?
hints: Bending a solid rod curves it along one line only.
Look for the design pressed in a mould.
questions.onCorrect: Pressing thin layers of wood in a mould gave curves in two directions at once, which neither bending nor carving could give at that price.

misconceptions.feedback: The No. 14 was bent from solid beech rods after steaming, and was not pressed from plywood in a mould.
The Anglepoise took its form from the springs that hold its arm in any position.
The SK 4 is a radio-phonograph known for its plain case and its controls grouped on one panel.

questions.prompt: Dieter Rams’s motto “less, but better” in German is “Weniger, aber ___”.
hints: The word is the German comparative of “gut”, good.
questions.onCorrect: The motto is a claim about quality: fewer elements, each one carefully worked out, and not simply fewer.

questions.prompt: What did Sullivan’s phrase “form ever follows function” ask of a designer?
hints: The word that matters in the phrase is “follows”.
Ask what the form follows.
questions.onCorrect: Form that follows function may turn out plain or not. What matters is that the shape can be traced back to a use.

misconceptions.feedback: Plain surfaces are one result a designer might reach, but the phrase says where form should come from, not that it should be bare.
The phrase is about letting purpose shape the thing, and not about hiding anything.
Sullivan’s phrase does not mention materials at all. It concerns the relation between purpose and shape.

choices.label: That a building should have no ornament
That the shape should arise from the purpose
That the function should be hidden from view
That everything should be made of the same material

acceptedIdeas: That the shape should arise from the purpose
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the shape should arise from the purpose

questions.prompt: A designer removes every control the user never needs and keeps the rest in one group. Which of Rams’s ten principles is this?
hints: Rams summed one principle up in the words “less, but better”.
questions.onCorrect: Rams summed this principle up as “less, but better”, since each element that remains has to be worked out with care.

misconceptions.feedback: Innovation concerns new technology or new ideas, while removing controls the user never needs is a matter of leaving out what is not essential.
Long-lasting concerns a design that stays useful and does not date. The change here reduces what the product has, not how long it serves.
Environmentally friendly concerns resources and pollution over the product’s life, while the change here concerns the controls a user meets.

acceptedIdeas: Good design is as little design as possible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Good design is as little design as possible

choices.label: Good design is as little design as possible

questions.prompt: In what year did Louis Sullivan write “form ever follows function”?
hints: It came after Thonet’s chair of 1859 and before the Bauhaus of 1919.
It was written near the end of the nineteenth century.
The year is in the 1890s.
questions.onCorrect: The phrase belongs to the architecture of tall steel-framed buildings, and it was later taken up by designers of objects.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the year of the Thonet No. 14 chair. The phrase is from Sullivan’s essay a few decades later.
That is the year the Bauhaus was founded, a generation after the phrase.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The phrase appeared in his essay on the tall office building in 1896.

questions.prompt: How many years lie between the founding of the Bauhaus in 1919 and the first iPhone in 2007?
hints: Subtract the earlier year from the later.
From 1919 to 2000 is 81 years.
Add the 7 years from 2000 to 2007.
questions.onCorrect: Even the earliest of these landmarks is far older than the last, and design was already a profession long before the iPhone.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a slip in the subtraction. Work from 1919 to 2000 and then add 7.
That is a slip in the subtraction. From 1919 to 2000 is 81 years.

questions.prompt: What did the Bauhaus, founded in Weimar in 1919, aim its students at?
hints: Think about how the objects its students drew were meant to be made.
questions.onCorrect: Teaching art and craft together and aiming both at production is why the Bauhaus belongs on a timeline of industrial design.

misconceptions.feedback: The Bauhaus aimed its students at objects drawn to be made in numbers, and not at one-off pieces made by hand.
The Bauhaus taught art and craft together, and pointed both at design for production.
The school’s aim was design for production, in which a shape answers to its use and to how it will be made.

acceptedIdeas: Design for production, so that a lamp or a chair was drawn to be made in numbers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Design for production, so that a lamp or a chair was drawn to be made in numbers

choices.label: Design for production, so that a lamp or a chair was drawn to be made in numbers

questions.prompt: The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919 by Walter ___.
hints: He was an architect.
questions.onCorrect: Gropius wanted a school in which art and craft were taught together and aimed at production by industry.

questions.prompt: A box has a small hook on its side wall that points sideways. The mould opens in one direction, straight up. Can the two halves part to release the box?
hints: Imagine the part sliding straight up out of the mould.
Which feature would catch on the mould as it moves?
questions.onCorrect: A feature like this is called an undercut, and it is dealt with by redesigning it or by adding a moving part to the mould, which costs more.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not help. A feature that points across the direction of opening is held by the mould however small it is.
Cooling longer makes the plastic stiffer, so the hook would be held more firmly, not released.
Every moulded part has walls. The problem is the one feature that points sideways, across the direction in which the mould opens.

choices.label: Yes, if the plastic is cooled for longer
Yes, because the hook is small
No, because the box has a wall
No, the hook locks the part in the mould

acceptedIdeas: No, the hook locks the part in the mould
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, the hook locks the part in the mould

questions.prompt: A face 50 mm long, parallel to the opening direction, is given a draft angle of 1.5 degrees. By how many millimetres does the face move over its length, to two decimals?
hints: The offset is the length of the face times the tangent of the draft angle.
tan 1.5° is about 0.0262.
Multiply 50 by it.
questions.onCorrect: The change is only a little over a millimetre, which is invisible on the finished part yet enough to let it release.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 50 × 1.5 divided by 100, which treats the angle as a percentage. Use the tangent of the angle.
That multiplies the length by the angle in degrees. Use 50 × tan(1.5°).

questions.prompt: A face 40 mm long has a draft of 1 degree. By how many millimetres does it move over its length, to two decimals?
hints: Offset = length × tan(angle).
tan 1° is about 0.01746.
Multiply 40 by it.
questions.onCorrect: A fraction of a millimetre is enough to free the face as soon as the mould starts to open.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 40 × 1 divided by 1000. Use the tangent of 1 degree, which is about 0.0175.
That is the length of the face, not its offset.

questions.prompt: A wall is 3.5 mm thick. Using a rib thickness of 0.6 of the wall, what is the rib thickness in millimetres, to one decimal?
hints: The rib is a fraction of the wall.
Multiply the wall thickness by 0.6.
questions.onCorrect: Keeping the rib thinner than the wall lets the plastic cool at about the same rate, so the face opposite it stays flat.

misconceptions.feedback: That makes the rib as thick as the wall. A rib that thick would show a sink mark on the other face.
That divides by 0.6. The rib is thinner than the wall, so multiply by 0.6.

questions.prompt: A shallow dent on the visible face above a thick section of plastic is called a ___ mark.
hints: Thick plastic cools and shrinks later than the thin wall around it.
The dent looks as if the surface has sunk.
questions.onCorrect: The thick region shrinks as it cools and pulls the surface in, which is why designers avoid thick sections behind visible faces.

misconceptions.feedback: Draft is the slight taper that frees the part. The dent over a thick section is a different defect, named for what the surface does as it cools.

questions.prompt: A boss is drawn as a solid cylinder 10 mm across on a 2.5 mm wall. To avoid a sink mark it is cored out so that its own wall is 0.6 of the nominal wall. What is the diameter of the hole, in millimetres?
hints: First find the boss wall: 0.6 of 2.5 mm.
The wall is on both sides of the hole.
Take twice the wall thickness from the 10 mm across.
questions.onCorrect: A cored boss is cooled like the rest of the part, and the same 0.6 guide is often used for the wall of a boss.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes off the boss wall on one side only. The wall is on both sides of the hole, so take it off twice.
That is the wall of the boss. The question asks for the hole inside it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The boss wall is 0.6 × 2.5 = 1.5 mm, on both sides of the hole. Hole = 10 − 2 × 1.5 = 7 mm.

questions.prompt: A face 30 mm long has a draft of 2 degrees. How far does it move over its length, in millimetres, to two decimals?
hints: Offset = length × tan(angle).
tan 2° is about 0.0349.
Multiply 30 by it.
questions.onCorrect: Doubling the draft doubles the offset, nearly exactly, for such small angles.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 1 degree. The draft here is 2 degrees.
That multiplies the length by the angle. Use the tangent of the angle.

questions.prompt: A wall is 3 mm thick and a rib is made 0.6 of the wall. What is the rib thickness, in millimetres?
hints: The rib is thinner than the wall.
Multiply the wall by 0.6.
questions.onCorrect: Ribs stiffen a wall without the thick section that would cause a sink mark.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wall thickness. The rib is a fraction of it.
That divides by 0.6. Multiply by it.

questions.prompt: A feature that points across the direction of opening and so locks the part in the mould is called an ___.
hints: The feature sits “under” the face the mould must pass.
questions.onCorrect: An undercut needs a slide or a core that moves sideways, which costs more, or else a redesign.

misconceptions.feedback: Draft frees a face. A feature that locks the part in is the reverse.

questions.prompt: A product has a case, two screws, a circuit board and a hinge, and nothing in it has to come apart for service. Applying the three questions, which parts could be merged into a neighbour or removed?
hints: Ask each part in turn: does it move, must it be a different material, must it be separate for assembly or service?
The first part always counts.
questions.onCorrect: The screws do not move, need no different material and do not have to come apart, so the theoretical minimum is three parts and a snap fit can do their job.

misconceptions.feedback: The hinge moves relative to the case, which is the first of the three questions, so it has to stay a separate part.
The circuit board has to be a different material from the case, with its own conductors and components, so it passes the second question.
The case is the first part, the base the others are placed on, and the first part always counts.

questions.prompt: The smallest number of separate parts that a product could have, judged by the three questions, is the theoretical ___ number of parts.
hints: It is the lowest count that still passes the questions.
questions.onCorrect: The theoretical minimum is a target to design towards. A product may need more parts for reasons the three questions do not capture.

questions.prompt: A product needs a theoretical minimum of 5 parts and takes 75 s to assemble. What is its assembly efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The ideal time is 3 s multiplied by the minimum number of parts.
The ideal time is 15 s.
Divide it by the actual time of 75 s.
questions.onCorrect: An index of 0.20 means one-fifth of the assembly time is spent on the ideal work, and the rest on handling, orientation and parts that need not be there.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 25 by 75. The ideal time is 3 s for each of the 5 minimum parts, which is 15 s.
That is the minimum part count. The index divides the ideal time by the actual time.

questions.prompt: After the redesign there are 5 parts, all of them needed, and the assembly takes 30 s. What is the efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The minimum number of parts is still 5.
The ideal time is 15 s.
Divide 15 by 30.
questions.onCorrect: The efficiency rose from 0.28 to 0.50 because the time fell by more than the part count did.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the efficiency before the redesign, 15 / 54. Use the new time of 30 s.
That would need the time to equal the ideal 15 s. The new time is 30 s.

questions.prompt: A cover is held on by two screws. Which change most reduces the assembly time while keeping the cover removable for service?
hints: A joint that is part of the cover itself adds no part.
The cover must still come off for service.
questions.onCorrect: Snap hooks are moulded with the cover, so the two screws and their handling disappear from the assembly.

misconceptions.feedback: More screws add parts to handle, orient and drive, each of which costs time.
A thicker cover does not change how many parts there are or how they are joined.
Tape adds a part and a step, and it makes the cover hard to remove again for service.

choices.label: Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded into the cover
Stick the cover on with tape

acceptedIdeas: Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded into the cover
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Replace the screws with snap hooks moulded into the cover

questions.prompt: The designer finds that the battery must be replaceable, so a separate battery door is added to the four-part design and kept, which makes the minimum 5 parts. The assembly now takes 27 s. What is the efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The ideal time is 3 s times the minimum number of parts.
The minimum is 5, so the ideal time is 15 s.
Divide 15 by 27.
questions.onCorrect: A requirement for service raises the minimum part count, and so it lowers the temptation to remove the door for the sake of the index.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 3 × 6 by 27. The minimum is 5 parts, so the ideal time is 15 s.
That divides 5 by 27, leaving out the 3 s ideal time for each part.

questions.prompt: A product needs a minimum of 5 parts and takes 60 s to assemble. What is its efficiency, to two decimals?
hints: The ideal time is 3 s times the minimum parts.
The ideal time is 15 s.
Divide it by 60 s.
questions.onCorrect: A quarter of the time is ideal work, and the rest is handling and extra parts.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides 5 by 60. The ideal time is 3 s for each minimum part.
That divides the time by the minimum count. The index is ideal time divided by actual time.

questions.prompt: A product has 12 parts and the theoretical minimum is 5. By how many parts could the design be reduced?
hints: Compare the actual count with the minimum.
Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: Every part removed also removes its handling, its orientation and its joining.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the minimum itself. The reduction is the difference between the actual and the minimum.
That adds the two. The reduction is found by subtracting.

questions.prompt: A product has 12 parts, and its theoretical minimum is 5. What does the difference of 7 tell the designer?
hints: The theoretical minimum counts the parts that pass at least one of the three questions.
questions.onCorrect: The minimum is a target rather than a promise, so each of the seven still has to be checked for a reason, such as service, to keep it separate.

misconceptions.feedback: A count of parts says nothing about time on its own, and the efficiency needs the measured assembly time as well.
Efficiency is 3 × N / t, the ideal time for the necessary parts over the real time, and it is not a ratio of part counts.
Parts that pass none of the three questions do not need to move. The point is that they could be combined with a neighbour or left out.

acceptedIdeas: Seven parts are candidates to be merged with a neighbour or removed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Seven parts are candidates to be merged with a neighbour or removed

choices.label: Seven parts have to be redesigned so that they move
The assembly efficiency is 7 divided by 12
Seven parts are candidates to be merged with a neighbour or removed
The assembly takes 7 seconds longer than it should

questions.prompt: In the efficiency calculation, the ideal time allowed for each necessary part is how many seconds?
hints: The index starts with a fixed time per part.
It is a few seconds.
It is the number that multiplies the minimum parts.
questions.onCorrect: Three seconds is the ideal time to pick up and fit a part that needs no care, and the index measures how far a real assembly is from that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one part, not the ideal time for it.
That is too long by a factor of ten.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The index is 3 s × minimum parts / actual time, so 3 s per part.

questions.prompt: To test whether a handle feels comfortable in the hand, which prototype is the right one to build?
hints: Ask which aspect of the product is being tested.
The prototype only needs to be as real as that aspect requires.
questions.onCorrect: A mock-up that matches the final handle in shape and size, and in nothing else, answers the question for very little money.

misconceptions.feedback: A production tool costs a great deal and takes months, and the question about the grip could have been answered long before it was made.
A picture can show how a handle looks, but nobody can hold it. The question is about how it feels.
Dimensions on a sheet do not tell a person how the handle feels. The aspect being tested is the feel in the hand, so something must be held.

questions.prompt: Each test user finds about 31 percent of the problems in a design, and different users tend to find some of the same ones. Roughly what share do two users find together?
hints: The second user finds some problems that the first did not, and repeats others.
The share found is less than the sum of the two.
questions.onCorrect: The share is 1 − 0.69² = 0.52, a little over half, which the next screen shows how to compute.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two shares, 31 + 31, which counts the problems that both users found twice.
That is the share for one user. A second user finds some problems that the first did not.
Two users are far from finding everything, since each finds only about a third and they overlap.

questions.prompt: Each user finds a fraction p = 0.31 of the problems. What fraction do n = 5 users find together, to two decimals?
hints: The fraction missed by one user is 1 − 0.31 = 0.69.
The fraction missed by five users is 0.69 to the power 5, about 0.16.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Five users find about 84 percent of the problems, and the sixth and seventh add much less than the first and second did.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 5 by 0.31, which counts overlapping problems several times and gives more than 1. The model is 1 − (1 − p)^n.
That is the fraction not found, 0.69⁵. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: How many users are needed to find at least 90 percent of the problems when p = 0.31?
hints: Try n = 6 and n = 7 in 1 − 0.69^n.
Six users find about 0.89.
The first n that reaches 0.90 is the answer.
questions.onCorrect: A fixed percentage of the problems needs more users each time the target is raised, and the cost rises faster than the benefit.

misconceptions.feedback: Six users find about 89 percent, which is just short of 90 percent.
Five users find about 84 percent, which is short of 90 percent.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 users find 1 − 0.69⁶ = 0.89, which is below 0.90, and 7 users find 1 − 0.69⁷ = 0.93, which is above. So 7 users are needed.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.31, what percentage of the problems do n = 3 users find, to the nearest percent?
hints: One user misses 0.69 of the problems.
Three users miss 0.69 to the power 3, about 0.33.
The share found is 1 minus that.
questions.onCorrect: Three users already find two thirds of the problems, so a small test is worth running.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 3 by 31. The model is 1 − 0.69³, which is much less than the sum.
That is the percentage missed, 0.69³, which is about 33 percent. Take it from 100.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.31, how many more percentage points of the problems do 15 users find than 5 users, to the nearest point?
hints: Work out the share found by 15 users, 1 − 0.69 to the power 15.
15 users find about 99.6 percent and 5 users 84.4 percent.
Subtract.
questions.onCorrect: Ten extra users add only fifteen points, and the same ten users could have run two more rounds on a design that had been corrected between them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share found by 15 users, not the difference from the share found by 5.
That is the share found by 5 users. Take it from the share found by 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 15 users find 1 − 0.69¹⁵ = 99.6 percent, and 5 users find 84.4 percent, a difference of 15.2, which is 15 points.

questions.prompt: With p = 0.31, what percentage of the problems do n = 4 users find, to the nearest percent?
hints: Four users miss 0.69 to the power 4.
That is about 0.23.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Each extra user adds less than the one before.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 4 by 31. The model is 1 − 0.69⁴.
That is the percentage missed. Take it from 100.

questions.prompt: Problems that are hard to find have p = 0.15. What fraction of them do n = 5 users find, to two decimals?
hints: One user misses 0.85 of such problems.
Five users miss 0.85 to the power 5.
Subtract it from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Problems that few users meet need more users or a test aimed at them.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies 5 by 0.15. The model is 1 − 0.85⁵.
That is the fraction not found. Subtract it from 1.

questions.prompt: How closely a prototype resembles the final product in the aspects being tested is its ___.
hints: It is the word for how faithful the prototype is.
questions.onCorrect: A prototype should have high fidelity only in the aspect being tested, and need not have it anywhere else.

questions.prompt: Product A takes 50 kg of CO2e to make and then causes 20 kg per year in use, for 5 years. Which stage carries more of its footprint?
hints: The use figure is per year, so total it over the life of the product.
Five years at 20 kg a year.
questions.onCorrect: The use phase is often larger than the manufacture, which is why counting only the making of a product can mislead.

misconceptions.feedback: Making is 50 kg, but five years of use add up to 5 × 20 = 100 kg, which is twice as much.
Making is 50 kg and use is 5 × 20 = 100 kg over the life, so the two are not equal.
The figures given are enough: compare 50 kg with the total for five years of use.

questions.prompt: Product C takes 60 kg of CO2e to make and causes 15 kg a year in use, for 6 years. What is its annualised footprint in kg a year?
hints: First find the whole-life total, making plus use for all the years.
Making 60, use 15 × 6 = 90.
Divide the total by 6.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing the whole-life footprint by the years of use puts a short-lived product and a durable one on the same footing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the use per year alone. The annualised figure adds the making, spread over the years.
That adds the making to one year of use and does not divide by the years. Total the whole life first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total = 60 + 15 × 6 = 150 kg. Annualised = 150 / 6 = 25 kg a year.

questions.prompt: Product B’s annualised footprint is 28 kg a year. For how many years must product A (50 kg to make, 20 kg a year in use) last to match it?
hints: A’s annualised footprint for n years is (50 + 20n)/n, which is 50/n + 20.
Set 50/n + 20 equal to 28.
Then 50/n = 8.
questions.onCorrect: A would have to last just over six years to match B, so a lifetime longer than the typical one would be a real design target.

misconceptions.feedback: At 5 years A is at 30 kg a year, which is above B’s 28. It must last longer.
That is the 8 kg a year by which A’s use falls short, not the number of years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A’s annualised footprint is 50/n + 20. Setting 50/n + 20 = 28 gives 50/n = 8, so n = 6.25 years.

questions.prompt: A repair that costs 5 kg of CO2e for a spare part extends product A (50 kg to make, 20 kg a year in use) from 5 years to 8 years. What is its annualised footprint now, in kg a year, to two decimals?
hints: The whole life is now 8 years, and the spare part adds 5 kg.
Divide the total by 8.
questions.onCorrect: Repair lowered the annualised figure from 30 to about 27 kg a year, even after counting the spare part.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure before the repair, with a 5-year life. Include the 5 kg for the part and the longer life.
That leaves out the 5 kg of the spare part, which also counts towards the footprint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total = 50 + 5 + 20 × 8 = 215 kg. Annualised = 215 / 8 = 26.875, which is 26.88 kg a year.

questions.prompt: Product B (80 kg to make, 20 kg a year in use) breaks after only 6 years. What is its annualised footprint, in kg a year, to two decimals?
hints: Find the whole-life total for 6 years.
Divide by 6.
questions.onCorrect: A longer-lived product is better only if it actually lasts, and a failure at 6 years turns a better design into the worse one.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B’s figure for a 10-year life. Here it lasts only 6 years.
That is the total for the whole life. Divide by the 6 years.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total = 80 + 20 × 6 = 200 kg. Annualised = 200 / 6 = 33.33 kg a year.

questions.prompt: Where the use phase dominates a product’s footprint, which is usually the best lever for a designer?
hints: Find the stage where most of the footprint lies.
Which change acts on that stage?
questions.onCorrect: A change that lowers the energy used each year is paid back every year of use, and it can outweigh savings in the materials.

misconceptions.feedback: Packaging belongs to the making and distribution stages, which are small when use dominates.
Recycling acts at the end of life, which is a small part of the footprint when use dominates.
Colour has no effect on the energy used. The stage that matters most is use.

questions.prompt: Product A (50 kg to make, 20 kg a year in use, 5 years) can be changed in one of two ways. Option 1 cuts making to 40 kg. Option 2 cuts use to 15 kg a year. How many kg a year lower is option 2 than option 1?
hints: Work out the annualised footprint of each option separately.
Option 1 gives 28 kg a year.
Option 2 gives 25 kg a year.
questions.onCorrect: The change to the use phase saves more, because the use phase is the larger part of the footprint.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the saving of option 1 alone, from 30 to 28. Compare the two options with each other.
That is the saving of option 2 alone, from 30 to 25. Take away the saving of option 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Option 1: (40 + 100)/5 = 28. Option 2: (50 + 75)/5 = 25. The difference is 3 kg a year.

questions.prompt: Product D takes 40 kg to make and causes 10 kg a year in use, for 8 years. What is its annualised footprint in kg a year?
hints: Find the whole-life total.
Making 40 plus use 10 × 8 = 80.
Divide by 8.
questions.onCorrect: The annualised figure is the quantity to compare, because lifetimes differ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the use per year alone. Add the making, spread over the years.
That is the making divided by 8, without the use.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Total = 40 + 10 × 8 = 120 kg. Annualised = 120 / 8 = 15 kg a year.

questions.prompt: For product D (40 kg to make, 10 kg a year in use, 8 years), what percentage of the whole-life footprint comes from the use phase, to the nearest percent?
hints: Find the use total, 10 × 8 = 80 kg.
The whole life is 120 kg.
Divide 80 by 120 and give a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: Two thirds of the footprint comes from use, so this is where D’s hotspot lies.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of making, 40 of 120. The question asks about use.
That is the use in kilograms, not a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Use = 80 kg of 120 kg in total, which is 66.7 percent, so 67.

questions.prompt: The stage of a product’s life where most of its impact sits is called its ___.
hints: It is the place to look first for a saving.
questions.onCorrect: Finding the hotspot tells a designer where a change will pay off, and where it will not.

questions.prompt: When should the weights in a concept matrix be set?
hints: Think about what a team could do with the weights after seeing the scores.
questions.onCorrect: Weights fixed in advance say what matters before anyone knows which concept they favour.

misconceptions.feedback: Weights set after the scores can be adjusted until a favourite wins, and the matrix then records a preference instead of a decision.
Seeing even one concept’s scores lets the weights be tilted towards or against it, so the weights have to come before any scoring.
Changing the weights to settle a disagreement about the winner amounts to choosing the winner first. Trying other weights belongs in a sensitivity check, done openly once the totals exist.

choices.label: After the first concept is scored, to give a reference
Whenever the team disagrees about the winner
After the concepts are scored, once their strengths are known

questions.prompt: All three concepts score 4 on a criterion called “meets the safety standard”. What does this criterion do to the ranking?
hints: Compute what an equal score adds to each concept.
If every total gains the same amount, the order does not change.
questions.onCorrect: A criterion that all concepts meet equally belongs in the brief as a requirement, and the matrix is left for the criteria that separate them.

misconceptions.feedback: A criterion on which every concept scores the same cannot decide between them. Whatever its weight, the same amount goes to each total.
The same score times the same weight adds the same amount to each concept, so no concept is lowered more than another.
A large weight would raise every total by the same amount and leave the order as it was. Meeting the standard is a requirement to be met by all.

choices.label: It should be given the largest weight
It adds the same amount to every concept, so it does not separate them
It lowers the total of the best concept most

acceptedIdeas: It adds the same amount to every concept, so it does not separate them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It adds the same amount to every concept, so it does not separate them

questions.prompt: The weights are 0.4, 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1 for cost, ergonomics, manufacture and sustainability. Concept B scores 3, 5, 4 and 4. What is its weighted total?
hints: Multiply each score by the weight of its criterion.
Add the four products.
questions.onCorrect: B totals 3.9 against A’s 3.7, so B leads on these weights.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the scores without the weights. Multiply each score by its weight first.
That is the plain average of the four scores. The weights make some criteria count for more.

questions.prompt: The first two weights are swapped, so they become 0.3, 0.4, 0.2 and 0.1. What is concept B’s total now?
hints: Multiply B’s scores 3, 5, 4 and 4 by the new weights.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: B’s lead has grown, because ergonomics, where B scores 5, now counts for more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B’s total before the swap. Use the new weights of 0.3 and 0.4 for the first two criteria.
That is concept A’s total after the swap. The question is about B.

questions.prompt: Now cost counts for far more: the weights are 0.7, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.1. What is concept B’s total, to one decimal?
hints: Multiply each of B’s scores 3, 5, 4 and 4 by its new weight.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: On these weights A totals 3.8, which is above B’s 3.4, so the winner has changed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is B’s total on the original weights. Use the new ones.
That is B’s cost score on its own. All four criteria count.

questions.prompt: If the winner changes when the weights are altered only a little, what does that say about the matrix?
hints: Ask how much the result depends on the weights.
A result that changes easily gives little reason to choose.
questions.onCorrect: A close result is the cue to discuss which criteria really matter and to look for more evidence, such as a test with users.

misconceptions.feedback: The arithmetic may be quite correct. The result shows that the concepts are close, which is information in itself.
The totals depend on the weights and scores, which are judgements. A result that flips with a small change should not be treated as final.
Nothing in the result points to bias. It shows that the two concepts are close on these criteria.

choices.label: It is final, since the totals are numbers
It is not decisive, so the choice needs more discussion
It is biased towards the first concept
It is wrong and must be redone

acceptedIdeas: It is not decisive, so the choice needs more discussion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is not decisive, so the choice needs more discussion

questions.prompt: Keep the other weights in the ratio 3 : 2 : 1 and give cost the weight w. Then A’s total is 3.5 + 0.5w and B’s total is 4.5 − 1.5w. At what weight on cost do the two totals become equal?
hints: Put the terms with w on one side.
Divide by 2.
questions.onCorrect: Above a weight of 0.5 on cost A wins and below it B wins, so the choice turns on how much cost matters, and that is worth discussing.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the largest weight possible. Solve 3.5 + 0.5w = 4.5 − 1.5w.
That is the original weight, where B leads. The totals meet at a larger weight.

questions.prompt: The weights are 0.5, 0.25, 0.15 and 0.1. Concept D scores 3, 4, 2 and 5. What is its weighted total, to one decimal?
hints: Multiply each score by its weight.
Add the four products.
questions.onCorrect: D’s strongest score is on the criterion with the smallest weight, so it adds less than it seems.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain average of the four scores. The weights make some criteria count for more.
That adds the scores. Multiply each by its weight first.

questions.prompt: Three weights are 0.35, 0.25 and 0.2, and the weights must add to 1. What is the fourth weight?
hints: The four weights add to 1.
The three given weights add to 0.8.
Take 0.8 from 1.
questions.onCorrect: Weights that add to 1 keep the totals on the same scale as the scores.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sum of the three given weights. The fourth makes the total 1.
That is the total of all four. Take away the three given ones.

questions.prompt: Changing the weights to see whether the winner changes is called a ___ check.
hints: It tests how sensitive the result is to the weights.
questions.onCorrect: A winner that survives sensible changes to the weights can be chosen with more confidence.

flashcards.front: The Double Diamond phases are discover, define, develop and ___.
flashcards.back: Deliver closes the second diamond with one tested design.

flashcards.front: Take "add a steel lid" and say, in your own words, the need it might stand for.
flashcards.back: A need says what the person must be able to do or what must hold, so it can be met by designs other than a steel lid.

flashcards.front: A right goal carried out with the wrong action is a slip. A wrong goal or plan is a ___.
flashcards.back: A mistake begins in the goal, so the fix is clearer information.

flashcards.front: Three knobs, three burners, one knob to one burner: how many assignments?
Mean 100 and standard deviation 10. What is the 95th percentile? (Give it to two decimals.)
Say why a doorway made for the average person fails, and which percentile it should use.
flashcards.back: Half of people are taller than the average, so a clearance has to be set from the large end, for example the 95th percentile.

flashcards.front: The law that gives choice time as b × log2(n + 1) is named after ___.
flashcards.back: Hick’s law says that choice time grows with the logarithm of the number of options.

flashcards.front: Distance equals width (D = W). What is the index of difficulty, in bits?
A ramp slope of 1:12 is the ___ allowed.
flashcards.back: The ratio is a limit, so any gentler slope also meets it.

flashcards.front: A turning space for a wheelchair is a circle 1525 mm across. How many inches is that, to the nearest inch?
In what year was the Bauhaus founded?
flashcards.back: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919.

flashcards.front: Say in your own words what “form follows function” does not mean.
flashcards.back: It does not mean plain or undecorated: it means that the form should arise from the purpose, whatever the result looks like.

flashcards.front: A slight taper on a moulded face, so the part releases from the mould, is called ___.
flashcards.back: Draft lets the faces slide away from the mould rather than rub as it opens.

flashcards.front: A wall is 2.5 mm thick. A rib is 0.6 of the wall. How thick is the rib, in millimetres?
A cover is held by two screws. A joint moulded into the cover that replaces them is a ___.
flashcards.back: A snap fit is part of the cover and needs no screw.
